title: Performance Without Guessing
summary: Programmers are famously bad at guessing where time goes. This lesson replaces guessing with measurement: frame budgets, **profilers** (Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool and sampling in general), microbenchmarks done properly, and the statistics that make timings trustworthy (medians and percentiles instead of averages). It ends with the common real causes of slow C++: cache misses, allocations, and work repeated every frame.
markdown:
## Budgets first "Fast enough" needs a number. A game at 60 frames per second has **16.7 ms per frame** for everything: input, simulation, rendering, audio, and the tools of chapter 12 if they are running. At 144 Hz it is 6.9 ms. A budget turns "it feels slow" into "the overlay takes 3.1 ms of our 16.7". For tools the budget is different (a memory scan should finish in under a second, an overlay should cost under 0.5 ms a frame), but it is still a number. ## Measure, then change one thing, then measure again ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Measure
(profiler or timer)"] --> B["Find the biggest cost"] B --> C["Change one thing"] C --> D["Measure again,
same conditions"] D -->|"better and still correct"| A D -->|"not better"| E["Revert it"] E --> B ``` Always measure **Release** builds (lesson 4.10: Debug builds can be ten times slower, and differently slow), on the same machine, with the same input, several times. ## Profilers A **sampling profiler** interrupts the program thousands of times a second and records which function was running. Functions that appear in many samples are where the time goes. In Visual Studio: **Debug → Performance Profiler → CPU Usage**, run the scenario, stop, and read the **Hot Path** and the list of functions sorted by **Total CPU** (including callees) and **Self CPU** (excluding them). Other useful tools: | Tool | Shows | |---|---| | Visual Studio CPU Usage | Where CPU time goes, by function and line | | Visual Studio Memory Usage | Allocations and their call stacks | | Windows Performance Recorder and Analyzer | Whole-system timelines: threads, waits, disk, GPU | | PIX | GPU and frame timing for Direct3D games | | An in-game frame timer | Per-system timings every frame, for regressions | ## Microbenchmarks done properly Sometimes you want to compare two versions of one function. Timing it naively lies in several ways: ```cpp #include #include #include #include #include volatile long long sink; // stops the optimiser removing the work long long sumVector(const std::vector& v) { return std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL); } int main() { std::vector data(1'000'000); std::iota(data.begin(), data.end(), 0); std::vector samples; for (int run{ 0 }; run < 25; ++run) { const auto start{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() }; sink = sumVector(data); const auto end{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() }; samples.push_back(std::chrono::duration(end - start).count()); } std::sort(samples.begin(), samples.end()); std::cout << "min " << samples.front() << " us, median " << samples[samples.size() / 2] << " us\n"; } ``` ```varies min 212.4 us, median 231.9 us ``` The rules it follows: - **Repeat** many times and look at the distribution; one run means nothing. - **Use the result** (here through a `volatile` variable) so the optimiser cannot delete the work. - Use **`steady_clock`**, which never jumps, not the wall clock. - Report the **median** and a high **percentile** (p95, p99), not just the mean: a single slow run caused by the operating system can pull the mean far away, while players feel the slow frames that the percentiles show. The practice task computes these. - Keep input sizes realistic: data that fits in the cache behaves completely differently from data that does not. ## The usual real causes When you do measure, the culprit in C++ is usually one of a short list: | Cause | Sign | Typical fix | |---|---|---| | **Cache misses** | Time in simple loops over large data; pointer-heavy structures (lesson 2.06) | Contiguous arrays, structure of arrays, smaller structs | | **Allocations in the frame loop** | `operator new` and `malloc` high in the profile | Reserve once, reuse buffers, pools (lesson 3.10) | | **Repeated work** | The same computation or lookup every frame | Cache the result; recompute only on change | | **Algorithmic cost** | Time grows much faster than input size | A better algorithm: hashing instead of searching, sorting once | | **Waiting** | Low CPU but slow; threads blocked | Profile waits (WPA); avoid blocking calls on the main thread | | **Debug-only overhead** | Fast in Release | Nothing to fix; measure Release | Note what is *not* on the list: rewriting clear code into clever code with no measurement. That rarely helps and often hurts. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Profiling Debug builds > You will optimise the wrong things. > [!warning] Trusting one timing > Run many times; report the median and a percentile. > [!warning] Benchmarks the optimiser deletes > If the result is unused, the compiler may remove the code and report it as free. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the measurement loop? - Change everything that might be slow, then measure once + Measure, change one thing, measure again, keep it only if better - Read the code, guess what is slow, and rewrite it in assembly - Measure in Debug, optimise, then ship > Changing one thing at a time is the only way to know which change helped. ? How does a sampling profiler work? - It adds timing code to every function at compile time - It runs each function on its own and times it + It records what code is running, many times a second - It counts how many lines each function has > Instrumenting every function is a different technique and slows the program much more. ? What are the usual real causes of slow C++ code? - Using `const`, references and small functions - Too many comments and long variable names + Cache misses, hot-loop allocations and poor algorithms - Using `std::vector` instead of raw arrays > `const`, references and comments cost nothing at run time. Repeated work, blocking waits, and measuring a Debug build are other usual culprits. ? What is the frame budget at 60 frames per second? + About 16.7 milliseconds - 60 milliseconds - 1 millisecond > 1000 ms divided by 60. ? Why report the median and p95 rather than only the mean? - The mean is harder to compute + A few slow runs skew the mean - Percentiles are always smaller > Distributions, not single numbers. ? Why store a benchmark's result in a `volatile` variable? - To make it run faster - To avoid cache misses + So the optimiser cannot remove the work > Unused results invite dead-code elimination. ```
ideas:
- Profile Delve with Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool and find its three most expensive functions.
- Benchmark an `std::vector<int>` sum against an `std::list<int>` sum of the same million values and explain the difference.
- Add a p95 frame time to Delve's frame timer.

cards.a:
Measure, change one thing, measure again, keep it only if better

Changing one thing at a time is the only way to know which change helped.
